To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a biokinetic-dosimetric model based on Michaelis-Mentin kinetics and a blocking mechanism is a valid tool to simulate the protective effect of iodine blockade after acute or continuous radioiodine intake.

a simple biokinetic-dosimetric model with a Michaelis-Metzen kinetic for iodine uptake and an additional total uptake blocking mechanism is able to simulate the protective effects of iodine blockade after acute or chronic radioiodine exposure.
the uptake of radio-iodine into the thyroid is saturable and that iodine blockade is effective in the case of acute exposure but less effective in case of continuous exposure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and validation of new biokinetic-dosimetric models for the simulation of iodine blockade and the optimization of antidote administration.
the development and validation of a biokinetic model of iodine blockade for the case of radioiodine exposure.
a new biokinetic model for radioiodine exposure and the application of the new model for simulation of radioiodine blockade.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the administration of stable iodine to block the uptake of radio-iodine is a very effective and useful measure to prevent thyroid cancer in case of nuclear accidents or other incidents.

a single dose of non-radioiodine is superior in the case of acute radioiodine intake, whereas in the case of continuous intake, a single dose is less effective and splitting the dose and shortening of dosage intervals enhance efficacy.
the efficacy of the iodine blockade is dose dependent and that the efficacy of a single dose is greater than the efficacy of a fractionated dose.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of a simple biokinetic model with Michaelis-Mentin uptake kinetics and total uptake blocking is sufficient to simulate the effect of iodine blockade.
the model-based simulation of iodine blockade in the case of radioiodine exposure in man is feasible.
the use of biokinetic-dosimetric models may contribute to the development of antidote dosage schemes and the improvement of emergency management.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the biokinetic-dosimetric modeling of iodine blockade is feasible and that the model is able to reproduce experimental data.
the efficacy of stable iodine administration depends on the time course of the radioiodine exposure.
the uptake mechanism of iodine into the thyroid gland is saturable, which is not accounted for by the standard biokinetic models.
